name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,380

clue.text: Features of a country walk perhaps lit up in three directions

definitions.text: Features of a country walk perhaps

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top
the short word sits inside the group of compass points

blocks.note: south, east and south again: three compass points
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rambler admires the features of a country walk lit up by the sun from several angles.
explanation.walkthrough: TIL sits inside S, E, S to give STILES.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiles are the steps over fences and walls that ramblers climb on footpaths, so they typify a country walk.

clue.text: Cologne can be so loud, with student festivity and shouting

blocks.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud
a rag is a British student charity festival
a rant is a loud harangue

explanation.surface: Someone's cologne is too strong, and the evening is noisy with student celebrations and yelling.
explanation.walkthrough: Cologne here is eau de cologne, the scent, not the German city.
explanation.definitionFit: Eau de cologne is a perfume, so it can be described as sweet-smelling; the clue gives an example of what has that quality.

clue.text: Left party upset, but another one's found

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so the letters are turned upside down in this down entry

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
Lab is short for the Labour Party

explanation.surface: A left-wing party is in turmoil, but a different party has been formed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another one' points back to 'party': the answer is a different kind of party, a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball is a grand formal dance, a social party rather than a political one.

clue.text: Tills continually annoy latest of customers moving to the end

indicators.note: the latest letter of a word is its final one
the letter is taken out of its place and set down again at the finish

blocks.note: to pester is to keep annoying someone
the final letter of customers

explanation.surface: Shop tills keep irritating the last shoppers in the queue.
explanation.walkthrough: PESTER loses its S, which goes to the back: PETERS. Peter is old criminal slang for a safe or cash box.
explanation.definitionFit: In thieves' slang a peter is a safe or till, so tills are peters.

clue.text: Bun hairstyle, unfamiliar on celebrity, turning heads

indicators.note: the heads of words are their opening letters
turning things over mixes up their order

blocks.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A celebrity with an unusual bun hairstyle makes people turn to look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bun hairstyle' reads as one phrase, but 'Bun' alone is the definition, a pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: A chou is a small round puff-pastry bun, as in choux buns filled with cream.

clue.text: Good music (pop) is something Italians devour?

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
rap is a genre of music
pop and pa are both words for father

explanation.surface: Good pop music is a passion Italians lap up eagerly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' in brackets looks like a gloss on music, but here it means dad.
explanation.definitionFit: Grappa is an Italian grape brandy; 'devour' is loosely stretched to drinking, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Perhaps look at white dwarf grasses around summerhouse, smell leaves

indicators.note: turned around, the word is read back to front
the smell departs, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: to rat is to inform, as a grass does
a gazebo is a garden summerhouse
BO is body odour

explanation.surface: A garden scene: white dwarf grasses around a summerhouse, with a smell drifting from its leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White dwarf' looks like a variety of ornamental grass; it is a kind of star. 'Grasses' are informers, and 'leaves' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A white dwarf is one kind of star, so gazing at it is one example of stargazing.

clue.text: Spades forced in damage group of trees

indicators.note: pushed into something, so the letter goes inside the other word

blocks.note: to hurt is to damage
S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: Spades are driven into the ground, harming a copse.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurst is an old word for a wooded hill or small wood, surviving in many English place names.

clue.text: Intolerable sentimentality that becomes Electra?

indicators.note: the answer turns into the name once its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the name from Greek tragedy, taken as written

explanation.surface: Syrupy sentiment that would suit a heroine of Greek tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: This works backwards: the answer, rearranged, becomes Electra.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacle is figuratively cloying, excessive sweetness of feeling, as in a treacly film or speech.

clue.text: Through short upland tract, carry grand piano

indicators.note: cut short, the word loses its final letter
one word passes through the middle of the other

blocks.note: a fell is a stretch of high moorland in northern England
to lug is to carry something heavy

explanation.surface: Removal men haul a grand piano across a stretch of hill country.
explanation.walkthrough: FEL, shortened, has LUG put through it. Flügel is German for a grand piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Flügel is the German word for a grand piano, named for its wing shape, and is used in English too.

clue.text: Did arm crack, training in middle of Sweden?

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters
the words sit inside the central letters

blocks.note: a crack is a witty remark
PE is physical education
the two central letters of Sweden

explanation.surface: A question of whether military training in central Sweden armed someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did arm crack' reads as a broken arm; 'Did arm' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To equip someone is to supply them with weapons or gear, so 'did arm' is the past tense, equipped.

clue.text: Pop star regularly eats starter of spare ribs, say

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every other one
the starter of a word is its opening letter
something eaten goes inside the eater

blocks.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
opening letter

explanation.surface: A pop star tucks into spare ribs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spare ribs' looks like the food; only 'ribs, say' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossa is the Latin plural of os, bone, and ribs are examples of bones.

clue.text: Film about graduates recalling construction of canal

indicators.note: calling back means the word runs backwards
constructing something means assembling the letters afresh

blocks.note: ca, circa, means about
BAs are Bachelors of Arts
taken as written

explanation.surface: A documentary about graduates reminiscing about building a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: Casablanca is the 1942 Bogart and Bergman film classic set in wartime Morocco.

clue.text: A pair of hecklers entering deceive Canadian singer-songwriter

indicators.note: a pair is two, taken from the front of the word
something entering goes inside

blocks.note: to con is to deceive
the first two letters

explanation.surface: Two hecklers sneak in to trick a Canadian performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pair of' takes just two letters from the front of hecklers, not the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonard Cohen was the Canadian singer-songwriter and poet behind 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne'.

clue.text: Contemporary artist dismissing unknown moneylenders

indicators.note: dismissing something sends it away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: Banksy is the anonymous British street artist
y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A modern artist fires some anonymous loan sharks.
explanation.definitionFit: Banks are the institutions whose business is lending money to borrowers at interest.

clue.text: Nervous wife brought in miniature

indicators.note: brought inside, the letter sits within the other word

blocks.note: titchy is British slang for very small
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A jittery wife has been brought into a tiny space.
explanation.definitionFit: Twitchy describes someone jumpy and anxious, given to twitching from nerves.

clue.text: Football team of 4, 8 and 27 saw the millions being mishandled

indicators.note: handled badly, the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A club where three named players watched millions being squandered.
explanation.walkthrough: Peters, Hurst and Moore were West Ham's three players in England's 1966 World Cup winning side.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Peters, Geoff Hurst and Bobby Moore all played for West Ham United, the East London club.

clue.text: Harmed native American cut and bloody

indicators.note: cut off, the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a dated, offensive term from old Westerns
blood is red

explanation.surface: Someone attacked, slashed and bleeding.
explanation.definitionFit: Injured and harmed are synonyms, both meaning physically hurt or damaged.

clue.text: One supports high-class pub with more senior following

blocks.note: U means upper-class
PH is the map abbreviation for public house
older means more senior in years

explanation.surface: A posh pub where an older crowd are loyal regulars.
explanation.definitionFit: An upholder is a person who maintains or backs something, such as a tradition or the law.

clue.text: English pals spread litter around walking areas

indicators.note: spread out, the letters are scattered into a new order
turned around, the word runs backwards

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written
a litter is a carried chair, like a sedan chair

explanation.surface: English friends scatter rubbish along the seafront promenades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' looks like rubbish; it is a carried couch, the sedan.
explanation.definitionFit: Esplanades are long open promenades, usually by the sea, laid out for strolling.

clue.text: Regular donations include a piece of bacon

indicators.note: the words include the answer, held within their letters

blocks.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Regular giving that includes a gift of bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: A lardon is a small strip or cube of fatty bacon used in cooking.

clue.text: No telephone boxes - little space

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it

blocks.note: to dial is to telephone
an en is a printer's unit of space

explanation.surface: A complaint that there are no phone boxes and not much room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No telephone boxes' reads as a shortage of kiosks; 'No' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A denial is a refusal or a negative answer, which is what saying no amounts to.

clue.text: Dog lead for Newfoundland kept in shed

indicators.note: the lead of a word is the letter that goes in front, its opening one
kept in something means held inside it

blocks.note: a hut is a shed
opening letter

explanation.surface: A Newfoundland dog's lead hangs in the shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog' is a verb here, to pursue, not a nod to the Newfoundland breed named in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to follow them persistently, as a hunter tracks prey.

clue.text: Given dope, play jazz aimlessly

blocks.note: first meaning: a fool
second meaning: to improvise idly on an instrument

explanation.surface: A musician on drugs just wanders around the tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given dope' suggests drugs; 'dope' is a dimwit.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is a silly person, and to noodle is to doodle musically with no clear direction.

clue.text: Daily officer serving London district

blocks.note: a daily or char is a British cleaning lady
Lt is short for lieutenant
on duty, serving

explanation.surface: A newspaper's officer on duty in a part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like a newspaper but is a cleaner. Charlton is in south-east London.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlton is a district of south-east London, home of Charlton Athletic football club.

clue.text: Character introducing The King, a musical act ending in 1977

indicators.note: the character introducing a word is its first letter

blocks.note: opening letter
rex is Latin for king

explanation.surface: An introduction to Elvis, the King, a performer whose career ended in 1977.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The King' and 1977 point to Elvis Presley, who died that year; so did Marc Bolan of T. Rex.
explanation.definitionFit: T. Rex was Marc Bolan's glam-rock band, which ended when he died in a car crash in 1977.

clue.text: Left-winger dominating victory embraces players

indicators.note: something embraced is held within

blocks.note: a decisive victory is a win
the London Symphony Orchestra, a body of players

explanation.surface: A left winger in football hugs his teammates after a crushing win.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Wilson was a Labour prime minister; Ray Wilson was England's left-back in 1966.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Wilson led the Labour Party, on the political left, and Ray Wilson played on England's left flank.

clue.text: Material John Wayne originally rejected

indicators.note: originally points to how a name begins, its opening letter
rejected things are sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: john is slang for a toilet
its first letter

explanation.surface: A fabric the actor John Wayne first turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: John Wayne is one name in the surface; split, 'John' is a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Wool is the yarn or cloth spun from sheep's fleece, a common material.

clue.text: Sculptor's way of working with brass abroad

blocks.note: MO, modus operandi, is a way of working
brass is slang for money, and the öre is a Scandinavian coin

explanation.surface: A sculptor's method of working in brass overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like the metal a sculptor casts; it is slang for money. Bobby Moore also captained West Ham.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Moore was the English sculptor famed for large reclining bronze figures.

clue.text: A loft towards the front stores meat primarily

indicators.note: heading to the front in an across entry means reading right to left
something stored is kept inside

blocks.note: taken as written
to loft a ball is to lob it
veal is calf meat

explanation.surface: An attic near the front of the house where meat is kept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A loft' looks like aloft or an attic; 'loft' is a verb, to lob.
explanation.definitionFit: Above all and primarily both mean first and foremost, most importantly.
